e.t: Abdemelech is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears four times, all in Jeremiah, in the LXX corpus. It is rendered as “Abdemelech” in the available English evidence, while “Avthemelekh” is also given as a gloss. The name is identified, but no further definition or surrounding verse text is provided here.

Abessalōm, also rendered Avessalom, is a proper name referring to a person rather than a word describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as a personal name 114 times, appearing most often in 2 Samuel and also in 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and 2 Maccabees. The name itself identifies the person; its particular significance in any passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative.

This Greek LXX noun means “leading.” It refers broadly to the act or role of guiding or directing rather than naming a specific person or place. Its central idea is movement under direction: someone or something is being led, or leadership is being exercised. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, including Esther and 2–3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Aisam is a proper name for a person; the same name is also given as Esam. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:50. Without the verse text or surrounding context, the name itself provides no further meaning beyond identifying the individual named there.

This adjective describes something that has no separate parts and cannot be divided. It expresses the idea of unity as a whole rather than something assembled from pieces. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains “without parts; indivisible.”

The word means “look up” or “see again.” It is a verb describing the act of directing one’s eyes upward or looking again so that something becomes visible. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 29 times, showing that it can describe ordinary physical looking rather than serving as a specialized religious term. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what the person is looking toward and the surrounding wording. The word appears from Genesis through 2 Maccabees, but its central idea remains renewed or upward sight.

This Greek LXX verb means “suffer,” describing the experience of enduring pain, hardship, or distress. It functions as an action word: it tells what someone undergoes rather than naming the person or difficulty itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 19:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the experience of suffering or enduring affliction.

This noun means “tolerance”: the willingness to endure or bear with something rather than respond with immediate rejection or resistance. It describes a capacity for patience or restraint, though its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding context. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 12:25. The available lexical meaning identifies the word clearly, while the verse reference alone does not provide enough surrounding text to explain the specific situation in which it is used.

This adverb means “from above” or “from the top.” It describes direction or position, pointing to something that comes down from a higher place or is located at the upper part of something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and Job. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what object, place, or movement the surrounding words describe.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “unapproachable” or “terrible”—not easily approached and inspiring fear or awe. It expresses a quality rather than an action, so its exact force depends on the person or thing it describes in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament translation represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:11. The word’s central sense remains the same: a presence so formidable that people shrink from coming near.

Ararat is a proper name identifying a place called Ararat. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Genesis 8:4, 2 Kings 19:37, and Jeremiah 28:27. The word functions as a place-name rather than a general description, action, or quality. It points readers to a named location, while the surrounding passage determines why that location is mentioned. The word itself does not carry a broader abstract meaning in the information available here.

This verb means “deny”: to refuse to acknowledge, affirm, or accept something. It describes a person rejecting a claim, statement, or position rather than agreeing with it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times: once in Genesis and five times in deuterocanonical writings, including Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what or whom the speaker refuses to acknowledge.

Arōni, also written Aroni, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in Nehemiah: 2:10 and 2:19. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish further meaning or significance beyond identifying the person who bears it.

Asaraddōn; Asaraththon is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 4:2. The available wording identifies the name itself, but the reference alone does not provide enough verse text to explain the person’s role or the surrounding conversation. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name Asaraddōn, also rendered Asaraththon.

Asennaphar, also rendered Asennafar, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not presented as an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily the identity carried by the name. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 4:10. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person’s role and significance there; the name itself functions as a personal designation rather than a general description.

“Aschōd; Askhoth” is a proper name preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:24. The available record identifies its name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the person, place, or family connection involved. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the genealogy’s immediate context, while the word itself functions as a specific name.

This noun means “courtyard” or “fold,” referring to an enclosed open area or a bounded place for animals. Its central idea is a defined space surrounded or marked off from what lies outside. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used broadly, occurring 179 times, so it can describe both built courtyards and animal enclosures depending on the surrounding passage. The exact sense in any verse is determined by that passage’s setting.

Aun, also rendered Avn, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 16:1. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its specific role in that passage cannot be explained further. The name itself identifies a person, while the surrounding biblical context would establish that person’s place in the account.

This proper name means “Babylōnia” or “Vavilonia,” referring to Babylonia. It names a place in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, appearing most often in Daniel, with additional occurrences in Isaiah and 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “dipping”: the act or process of putting something into a liquid or other substance. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Psalms and once in Sirach. The surrounding words in each passage determine what is being dipped and why. It should therefore be understood as a reference to the act of dipping, without adding a more specific object or purpose not stated here.

This is a proper name identifying people or a person called “Bērōthaios” or “Virotheos.” It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs twice, both in 2 Samuel: 4:3 and 23:37. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise reference in each passage cannot be explained further, but its basic function is to identify someone by name or designation.

Gazara is a proper name for a place, rendered “Gazara” in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographic designation. This name occurs ten times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Joshua, 1 Chronicles, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Because it identifies a location, its specific significance in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and the events connected with that place.

This word means “milk,” the nourishing substance referred to as food in the Greek Old Testament. It is a noun naming milk directly, whether mentioned in ordinary meals or in descriptions of a fertile land associated with abundance. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, showing a consistent, concrete meaning rather than an abstract idea. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “joking”—speaking or behaving in a playful, unserious way rather than treating something as a serious matter. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 19:14. The word describes an action, so it identifies what someone is doing in speech or conduct. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is straightforward: treating something as a joke or speaking playfully.

This adjective describes something that is known or can be known. It points to what is recognizable, understood, or made clear rather than remaining hidden or beyond knowledge. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 18 times, so it is used across several passages to identify people, things, or matters that can be recognized or understood. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “tear,” referring to the drop that comes from the eye, often expressing grief, distress, or deep feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 33 times, including passages from Psalms, Jeremiah, Lamentations, and Isaiah. Its basic sense remains physical, while the surrounding verse determines whether the tear reflects pain, mourning, prayer, or compassion.

This Greek LXX verb means “conclude”: to bring something to an end or complete it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek text of the Septuagint tradition represented here, in 2 Maccabees 12:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are needed to explain what was concluded.

This verb means “peep out” or “lean out.” It describes someone looking or extending themselves outward from a place of concealment or enclosure, so the central idea is a cautious movement into view. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:19. The surrounding verse would determine exactly who is doing this and what prompted the action.

This Greek LXX verb means “dedicate”: to set something apart for a particular purpose. It describes an action of formally giving or committing something for use, often in a sacred or public setting. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, so its basic sense is established across repeated scriptural usage rather than a single passage. The precise force in any verse depends on what is being dedicated and the surrounding context.

This word means “leader of a hundred” or “centurion,” a person commanding a unit of about one hundred soldiers. As a noun, it identifies a military officer rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 22 times, including passages describing the organization of Israel’s people and army. Its basic meaning remains connected to authority over a hundred, while the precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut out”: it describes removing or severing something by cutting. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including Isaiah and the books of Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being cut and the surrounding sentence.

Elisur is a personal name, rendered “Elisur” or “Elisour.” In the Greek Old Testament, it refers to a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs five times, all in Numbers, from Numbers 1:5 through Numbers 10:18. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular role in each reference cannot be described further, but its basic function is clear: it identifies a person by name.

This verb means “fall in,” describing someone or something moving into a place, situation, or position, often by falling. In the Greek Old Testament, it can express entering or being caught in circumstances, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise sense. It occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, so it is used for more than one kind of falling or entering.

This Greek LXX verb means “send in.” It describes the act of causing someone or something to enter or be placed inside. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Baruch and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on what is being sent and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains directed entry: someone sends another person or thing inward rather than merely moving it generally.

gl: buy out; make the most of
d: buy out; make the most of

e.h: Buy Out or Make the Most
e.t: This verb means “buy out” or “make the most of,” describing an active effort to obtain the greatest possible use or advantage from an opportunity. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:8, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains purposeful action: securing something or using an opportunity wisely rather than letting it pass unused.

This Greek LXX verb means to adorn or deck out—to make something more attractive or suitably arranged by adding decoration. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its meaning focuses on beautifying or preparing something outwardly. The word occurs twice in the Greek text of 4 Maccabees, appearing in 4 Maccabees 5:23 and 13:24. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This Greek LXX noun means “exodus,” referring to a departure or going out. It can name the act or event of leaving, especially when people move away from one place. The word occurs 64 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, so it is a recurring term rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective describes something as “laborious” or “tiring”—requiring effort, causing weariness, or being difficult to endure. It can describe work, a task, or any experience marked by strain and fatigue. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:7. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the adjective describes there, but its basic meaning remains a burden or activity that demands effort and leaves one weary.

This word means “pursuit”—something a person seeks, follows, or devotes effort to. As a noun, it can describe an aim or chosen endeavor rather than an action viewed moment by moment. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 53 times, showing that it is a recurring term for what people pursue or practice. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject, but its central idea remains a directed pursuit or undertaking.

Ermōni is a proper name, rendered “Ermōni” or “Ermoni,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a personal name in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in 2 Samuel 21:8. Because it is a name rather than a descriptive term, its meaning is chiefly its identification of the person named, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific context.

This verb means “crawl,” describing movement close to the ground rather than ordinary walking or running. It can refer to creatures that move by creeping along, and its precise force is shaped by the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, including passages in Genesis and Leviticus. The word therefore presents a straightforward picture of low, creeping movement, whether describing animals or another subject that advances in this way.

This noun refers to nobility of birth or high descent—an honorable standing connected with a person’s family origin. It describes inherited social distinction rather than an action or emotion. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. The central idea remains elevated birth or noble lineage, while the surrounding passage determines how that status is being discussed.

This adjective describes something that is “easy to pass.” It presents a way, route, or passage as accessible rather than difficult to move through. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs six times, appearing in Genesis, Numbers, Judges, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being described, but its central idea remains straightforward access or movement through something.

This word means “live” or “alive.” As a verb, it describes being alive, continuing to exist, or living rather than being dead. It is a broad and frequently used word in the Greek Old Testament, appearing 494 times across the Septuagint corpus. Its use extends from living creatures and people to the continuing life of individuals or communities. The precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This adjective describes something that has been only partly boiled or cooked, rather than fully prepared. It refers to an incomplete cooking process and therefore presents something as unfinished in its condition. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Isaiah 51:20. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise force in that passage cannot be described beyond this basic meaning. The word’s central idea remains clear: something is only partially cooked, not completely done.

Ietheraam is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily the individual it names rather than a broader concept. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 3:5. The available information identifies the name clearly, but the verse text is needed to explain the person’s role or significance in that passage.

This word refers to a supplication: a humble, earnest request made to someone from whom help or a response is sought. It functions as an adjective, describing something connected with such pleading. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it appears twice—once in Job and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense is therefore focused on the act or character of earnest entreaty, while the surrounding passage determines what is being requested.

This is a proper name: “Ioppitēs; Ioppitis.” It identifies a person or group by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees, at 2 Maccabees 12:3 and 12:7. The available information establishes its naming function and form, but not the specific identity or role of the person or people named in either passage.

Iōaa is a proper name, rendered as “Iōaa” or “Ioaa.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 26:4. Without the verse text or surrounding passage, the name itself gives no further meaning beyond identifying the individual called Iōaa. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding genealogy and context.

Ioach is a personal name, rendered as “Iōach” or “Ioakh.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs four times: once in 1 Chronicles and three times in Isaiah. The available references show that it is used as an individual’s name, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so those references do not establish additional meaning or details about the people who bore it.

This verb means “take down” or “demolish”—to bring something standing to the ground or remove it from its place. It can describe the physical destruction of an object or structure, and its use across the Greek Old Testament shows that it expresses an act of tearing down rather than merely moving something. The word occurs 87 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, so its basic sense is well established across many passages.

This Greek LXX noun means “cornstalk,” referring to the tall, stiff stalk of a grain plant. It names a physical plant stem rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including passages from Exodus, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a dry or standing stalk associated with grain or vegetation.

This noun refers to thinking ill of someone or regarding that person as low. It describes a negative judgment or low estimation of another person. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Sirach 5:14. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning centers on holding another person in low regard or thinking badly of them.

This word means “trampling” or “treading”—the act of stepping forcefully on something or walking over it. It is a noun that describes such an action, and it can also function adjectivally to characterize something marked by trampling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times across ten verses, including passages in Isaiah, Daniel, Ezekiel, Lamentations, and Micah. Its central idea remains the physical action of being trodden down or walked upon; the surrounding verse determines whether the word describes an act, condition, or image.

This Greek word means “destruction” or “death.” As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it refers to ruin, deadly loss, or the end brought about by destruction. It occurs six times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Chronicles, Esther, Psalms, Daniel, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. The precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is the removal or collapse of life, strength, or security.

“By lot” means in a manner determined by casting or using lots, rather than by ordinary choice or personal assignment. It is an adverb, so it describes how an action or distribution takes place. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word appears four times, all in Joshua 21, where the surrounding passage concerns the distribution of designated cities. The word itself states the method—by lot—while the passage supplies the particular outcome.

This noun means “cutting down; slaughter,” referring to the act of bringing people or things down by force. It presents destruction as an action rather than naming a person or place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 10:20. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of cutting down or slaughter. This is a distinct Greek LXX word, and its meaning is stated directly by these terms.

This Greek LXX noun means “dog fly,” referring to a kind of fly. It names an insect rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, with most occurrences in Exodus and additional occurrences in Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains the name of this fly.

This Greek LXX word means “lord” or “master,” referring to one who holds authority or has the right to direct others. It can describe a human master or be used as a title for God, depending on the surrounding passage. As a noun or adjective, it identifies someone as having lordship, authority, or ownership. It is very common in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, occurring 7,822 times, so its precise force is determined by the person or authority being addressed.

e.h: Covered or Like a Covered Chariot
e.t: This adjective means “like a covered chariot” or “covered.” It describes something having a covering or resembling a covered vehicle. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 7:3, so its normal meaning is shown by this single recorded use rather than by a broad range of passages. The word itself describes a quality or appearance; the surrounding verse determines exactly what object it modifies there.

This Greek LXX noun means “whiteness,” referring to the quality or appearance of being white. It names a visible characteristic rather than an action or person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Sirach 43:18. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition of being white or pale in appearance.

This LXX noun means a “censer,” a vessel used for carrying or burning incense. It names an object rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in 1 Chronicles 9:29 and once in 3 Maccabees 5:2. Those references show its limited usage, while the basic meaning remains the same: a censer associated with incense.

Maasias is a proper name, referring to a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Maasias” and occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Nehemiah, at 12:41 and 12:42. The available lexical information presents this word chiefly as an identifying name; its precise personal reference belongs to the surrounding passage rather than to the name itself.

Mallo is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 12:21. The name itself does not reveal the person’s character, role, or significance; those details must come from the surrounding verse and passage. Here, Mallo functions simply as a personal name.

Marēsa is a proper name, also represented as “Marisa.” It identifies a person or place by name rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:21. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its particular referent cannot be identified beyond this naming function. The name itself should therefore be read as a designation, with the passage supplying the specific person or place intended.

This Greek LXX verb means “boast” or describes someone as a “boaster.” It expresses proud, self-important speech rather than humble or modest words. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Ezekiel 35:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the context there. Its basic sense remains speech marked by boasting or proud self-assertion.

“Moderately” describes something done or present to a limited, balanced, or not extreme degree. As an adverb, the word modifies an action or description by showing its extent rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 15:38. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a measured degree rather than excess or intensity.

This adjective describes someone who can hardly speak or is unable to speak. It points to impaired or absent speech rather than expressing a general idea about silence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 35:6, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains a person who is speech-impaired or dumb.

A welt is a raised mark or swelling on the body, ordinarily associated with an injury. It is a noun naming the visible result of a blow or wound rather than the action itself. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs eight times across seven verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a welt: an outward bodily mark caused by harm.

This verb means “make foolish” or “turn into foolishness.” It describes causing someone or something to become foolish rather than merely identifying foolishness as a quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 44:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an action that produces foolishness or renders something foolish.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Nai” or “Ne.” It is not presented as a general description, action, or quality, but as an identifying name in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs five times, in five verses, from Genesis through Isaiah. Its exact reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a personal designation.

Nechaō, also rendered Nekhao, is a proper name—the personal name of a person mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general concept; it identifies someone in the biblical narrative. This name occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 10 verses, beginning in 2 Kings 23:29 and continuing through Jeremiah 26:17. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This noun means “drought” or “dryness”: a condition in which moisture is absent or greatly reduced. It can describe dry ground, a lack of rain, or another state of being parched. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, including several passages in Judges and Ezekiel. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is described as dry and on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “make one’s own”: to take something or someone as belonging to oneself. It describes an act of claiming, adopting, or treating something as one’s own rather than merely observing or encountering it. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 5:26. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the act of making something one’s own.

This LXX word refers to disparaging speech or reproach directed against someone. As a noun, it describes the shame, insult, or verbal disapproval expressed toward a person rather than an action of speaking itself. It is used 67 times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, most often rendered “reproach.” Its repeated use shows a broad term for the burden or offense of being spoken against, especially in passages where a person or people endure public dishonor. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

Orphanhood means the condition of being without parents or parental care. As a noun, it names that state of loss and vulnerability rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 47:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition of orphanhood. The word therefore points to the experience or status of those left without the protection and care normally provided by parents.

This Greek LXX noun means “earthenware,” referring to an object made from baked clay. It describes something formed from earthy material and therefore ordinary, breakable, and comparatively fragile. The word appears 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including several uses in Daniel. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a clay vessel or earthen object.

This adjective describes someone or something as “bitten by a snake.” It identifies the condition caused by a snake’s bite, rather than naming the snake itself or describing a general danger. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 12:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its precise role in that sentence depends on the context, but its basic meaning remains clear: affected by a snake bite.

This verb means “beget children”—to father or bring children into being. It describes the act of producing offspring rather than simply referring to children themselves. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:25. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific force there, but the word’s basic meaning remains the act of begetting children.

This Greek LXX verb means “embrace” or “admit”—to receive someone or something willingly, or to accept it as true or acceptable. It describes an active response rather than merely noticing or encountering something. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Exodus, Proverbs, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This verb means “stretch along,” describing an action in which something extends lengthwise along a line or area. It focuses on the way something reaches outward or continues across a space, rather than naming an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, each in a different verse. Its central meaning remains consistent, while the surrounding passage determines what is being extended and how that action functions in the sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “stop”: to bring an action or activity to an end, or to cease doing something. It describes stopping as an act, rather than naming a person or thing. The word appears 69 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used broadly for the ending of actions or ongoing events. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being stopped and the surrounding context.

This word means “bake.” It is a verb describing the act of preparing food by baking it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus, at Leviticus 6:10 and Leviticus 23:17. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: something is made ready through baking. The surrounding words determine what is being baked and how the action functions in each passage, but the word itself refers to the baking process rather than to a person, object, or abstract idea.

This noun refers to a cover or wrapping—something placed around or over another object. It describes a physical covering rather than an action or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within the books of Numbers and Judges. The exact force in any particular sentence depends on what is being covered and the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a material cover or wrapping.

Persis is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times: once in Daniel and nine times in the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise reference must be determined from each passage. The name appears in Daniel 11:2 and in several passages in 1 Maccabees.

This noun refers to an evergreen oak, specifically an ilex, a type of tree that remains green throughout the year. Its meaning is botanical and concrete: it identifies the tree itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Susanna 1:58. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact role in that sentence must be understood from that passage’s context.

This verb means to stoop to, describing a downward bending or lowering oneself toward something. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:27. The reference identifies where the word appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific action in that passage. Its central meaning remains the act of stooping or bending toward something.

This verb means to fall against someone or at someone’s feet, describing movement toward the feet of another person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it refers to physically falling against or arriving at a person’s feet. The word occurs 18 times in this LXX corpus, showing repeated use of this central idea. The surrounding passage determines the particular circumstance, but the basic meaning remains falling against or at the feet rather than simply standing nearby.

This noun means “gate”: an entrance or passage used to enter or leave a place. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it refers to gates as physical features of cities, buildings, or other enclosed places. The word occurs 46 times, so it describes a familiar part of the built environment rather than a rare or specialized object. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a gate or doorway-like entrance.

Roōb, also rendered Rhoov, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or place named Roōb. The name appears three times, in 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its basic function remains that of a personal or place name. The spelling may appear slightly differently in English because transliteration represents the Greek name rather than translating it.

This proper noun refers to a Samaritan, a person identified with Samaria. Its lexical gloss is “Samareitēs; Samaritis,” naming the person rather than describing an action, quality, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 17:29. Because the word is a name for a people or person associated with Samaria, the surrounding verse supplies the particular setting in which it is used. It should therefore be understood primarily as an identifying name.

Sachar, also rendered Sakhar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:35, identifying a person by name. The name itself is the central meaning available here; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s specific role or significance in the passage. This LXX form should be understood as a personal designation, not expanded into an additional meaning.

Sellēsa is a proper name, also represented as Sellisa. It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 16:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific referent in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its identity as the name Sellēsa or Sellisa.

In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this noun means “heap of ashes” or “ashes.” It refers to the remains left after something has been burned, especially when gathered into a pile. The word appears four times in the LXX, in Leviticus and Numbers, and its English rendering is consistently “ashes.” Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “warp,” the set of threads arranged lengthwise in woven cloth. It names part of a textile rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, all in Leviticus 13, where the surrounding subject is cloth being examined. Its basic meaning remains the textile structure called the warp; the precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This adjective means “shut up,” describing something closed, confined, or prevented from being open or accessible. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 7:36. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this basic sense. Its central idea is being shut in or closed off rather than open or freely available.

This noun describes a false accuser or slanderer—someone who brings damaging charges or speaks against another without truth. It names a person rather than the act of accusing itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, in Psalms and Proverbs, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse wording is not provided here. The word points to harmful, unjust speech that misrepresents another person.

This Greek LXX verb means “congregate” or “collect”: it describes bringing people or things together into one gathering. As an action word, it focuses on the act of assembling rather than on the group itself. It occurs 32 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what—or whom—the surrounding passage says is being gathered.

This noun refers to an event or fate—something that happens or comes upon a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe an occurrence considered as part of what unfolds in life, whether favorable or difficult. The word appears nine times in seven verses, with most occurrences in Ecclesiastes, where it is rendered “event.” Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “throw all together into confusion” or “confound.” It describes causing people or circumstances to become confused, disturbed, or thrown into disorder. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 13 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Old Testament books and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “thong,” referring to a narrow strip or band of material. It is used seven times in the Greek Old Testament, including descriptions of the lampstand and its connected parts in Exodus 25. The word therefore identifies a physical strip or band used as part of an object, rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description of the object.

Tabek, also rendered Tavek, is a proper name. It identifies a person or named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Genesis 22:24. The available lexical definition preserves the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or description. Its precise role in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage and the person named there.

Tephōn, also rendered Tefon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Maccabees 9:50. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or other named entity; its precise identification must come from that passage’s context.

e.h: A Word for Do For The Third Time
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “do for the third time”. It describes an action repeated until it has occurred three times. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Kings 18:34. The word therefore focuses on repetition and the completion of a third performance, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific action being repeated.

This Greek LXX verb describes someone as delicate or dainty. It points to a refined, tender, or physically delicate manner rather than naming a person or object itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Esther 5:1, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being described.

This noun refers to an “under-trough” or “vat,” a container positioned beneath something to hold liquid. It names a physical vessel rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Isaiah, Joel, Haggai, and Zechariah. The basic sense remains that of a vat or lower trough, while the surrounding verse determines what liquid or activity is associated with it.

This noun means “murderer,” a person who deliberately kills another person. It identifies someone by the act of unlawful killing rather than describing a general enemy or violent person. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, the word occurs once, in Wisdom 12:5. The exact force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the people being discussed.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Chaldaia; Khalthea.” It is not a general description or action word, but a specific name used in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Jeremiah 27:10. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be explained further here; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself and its proper-noun function.

This word is a proper name rendered “Chalchal” or “Khalkhal.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise identity in that genealogy cannot be described further; the supported meaning is the name itself and its function as a proper noun.

This Greek LXX verb means “storm-tossed”: being driven or shaken by a storm. It describes a condition of upheaval caused by violent weather rather than a person’s deliberate action. In the LXX, it occurs once, in Proverbs 33:10. The word’s basic picture is of something caught in storm conditions and subjected to their force. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its comparison or imagery, but the central idea remains being buffeted and unsettled by a storm.

Chorraios, also rendered Khorreos, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person or people by name rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. The name occurs seven times in seven verses within the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Joshua. Because no verse text or broader context is supplied here, its precise referent in each passage cannot be described further, but its basic function is to designate Chorraios or Khorreos.

“Anointing” refers to the act of applying oil, especially in a sacred setting. This noun describes the anointing associated with the worship practices and holy things presented in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs 15 times in 14 Old Testament verses, appearing most often in Leviticus and Exodus. The word therefore points to an act of consecration or preparation rather than to the oil alone. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Ōdoue is a personal name, represented in English as “Ōdoue” or “Othue.” It does not function as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:24, so its meaning is chiefly its role as the name of a person rather than a broader vocabulary concept. The surrounding verse would be needed to identify the individual or explain the name’s particular place in that passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called Ōrēr, also rendered Orir. It is not a word describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual idea; its function is to identify an individual. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:15. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the name itself establishes identity without supplying further information about the person or the event.
